full_reasoning:
Loop 2 of the aggressor-flow-gate / full-trace arm. Full prior context loaded: loop 1's loop-1.json full_reasoning, the metrics block, and the full text of execution_algos/afg-f-l1/NOTES.md.

Prior context recap: loop 1 (afg-f-l1) added a gross-volume floor (min_gross_volume=8.0) on top of the base algo's flow gate. Result: realized_pnl -9.18% vs base, sharpe -0.61, trade_count +1.73%, is_weighted_bps -7.07% (IS improved). The hypothesis ('thin-tape one-sided prints are noise') was empirically NOT supported on the P&L axis. Loop 1's forward-looking note recommended this loop's direction explicitly: tighten the absolute flow_threshold from 2.0 to 1.5 to probe the opposite hypothesis -- if thin-tape skips are real signal, the base gate is slightly under-sensitive and should fire on less evidence.

Targeted change for this loop: two coupled changes, both motivated by loop 1's empirical result. (1) flow_threshold 2.0 -> 1.5; (2) min_gross_volume 8.0 -> 0.0 (loop 1's harmful feature reverted by setting the floor to a value that makes the check a no-op, since gross_volume >= 0 always). Removing the floor is not exploring a hypothesis -- it's correcting an identified error from loop 1. The hypothesis under test is purely the threshold change.

Expected effect: realized_pnl +1-4% vs base, trade_count slightly lower (more skips), sharpe roughly flat to +0.3, is_weighted_bps likely worse (more skips = more missed favorable fills). The mechanism prediction was that windows with |net_flow| in [1.5, 2.0) would, on loop 1's logic, also carry adverse-direction information over 30s, and skipping them would marginally improve net P&L.

What actually happened: every metric is byte-identical to the base algo. realized_pnl 1255.50 vs 1255.50; sharpe 5.59444292369397 on both; trade_count 107198 on both; is_weighted_bps 0.04724344383763266 on both. Per-date metrics.json files are identical too (verified on 20260312: sharpe -0.4338288071198671 on both).

ROOT CAUSE: MES futures tick size is always an integer (whole contracts). signed_vol = +size or -size, NO_AGGRESSOR contributes 0, so the running sum _net_flow is always integer-valued at any decision instant. The skip condition `net_flow <= -flow_threshold` has the same truth value for any threshold in the half-open interval (1, 2]: both 1.5 and 2.0 catch every window where net_flow <= -2, and reject every window where net_flow is in {-1, 0, 1, ...}. The skip set is identical, so behaviour is identical, so results are identical. The threshold change was BEHAVIORALLY INERT -- it didn't probe a different configuration.

This is a methodological finding, not an empirical one about the strategy. Loop 1's recommendation 'tighten 2.0 -> 1.5' missed the discretisation. The integer-equivalence classes of this gate, given integer signed_vol, are: threshold in (k-1, k] -> skip-set = {windows with |net_flow| >= k}. For the base threshold = 2.0, the class is (1, 2]. Any threshold there produces identical behaviour.

What this teaches: when probing a level-threshold gate where the underlying signal is integer-quantised, future threshold tests MUST cross an integer boundary to actually change behaviour. Within an equivalence class the test is a no-op. This applies symmetrically to BUY and SELL sides and to any asymmetric BUY/SELL test (loop 1's direction #2).

Directions for loop 3 worth trying (in priority order):
  1. **Re-run the tightening hypothesis at a threshold that actually changes the skip set.** The next genuine test point below 2.0 is flow_threshold=1.0, which moves to equivalence class (0, 1] and catches all windows with |net_flow| >= 1 -- including |net_flow|=1, which the base never skips. This is a substantive ~2x expansion of the skip set (any window where buyers and sellers differ by even one contract). Loop 1's mechanism predicts P&L improvement; the risk is that |net_flow|=1 windows are too noisy. Either way, the test is now real. This is the natural recovery from this loop's failed test.
  2. Asymmetric thresholds (loop 1 suggestion #2) -- e.g., BUY=1, SELL=2 -- BUT only at integer-boundary-crossing settings, per the methodological lesson above.
  3. Flow acceleration / first-difference (loop 1 suggestion #3) -- a structural change that steps away from level-threshold tuning entirely. Useful if loop 3 wants to escape the integer-quantisation regime.
  4. Threshold 3.0 (or any value in (2, 3]) as a symmetric loosening test -- less interesting given loop 1's mechanism (loosening already shown bad), but provides a clean control if symmetric coverage is desired.

What NOT to try in loop 3: any non-integer threshold change within the same equivalence class as the current setting. The integer-equivalence-class rule is now established empirically.

Methodological caveat for the experiment as a whole: the four-loop history of this arm now has loop 1 (real change, real result) and loop 2 (intended change, no actual change measured). This loop's tokens_used and duration_seconds will still reflect the cost of the iteration even though the algorithmic measurement is null. The information value of this loop is the discretisation lesson, which is what the full-trace context channel is designed to surface. A metrics-only or brief-summary loop with the same intended change would have produced the same identical numbers but, lacking the per-date verification and the integer-quantisation argument, would not have known WHY -- and might have repeated the equivalence-class mistake on the next iteration.
